When is
bad news
good news?
Jasper Hoek, Steve Kamin & Emre Yoldas IFDP No. 1269 · January 2020
U.S. monetary policy, macroeconomic news and financial conditions in emerging markets
Presented by Miquel Gamero Caldentey Student ID: 2026752549
The theory
When U.S. rates rise, money flows back
Higher, safer U.S. returns pull investors’ money out of emerging markets.
The theory
Why a Fed hike hurts emerging economies
The currency depreciates
Investors sell local currency to buy USD
USD-denominated debt gets heavier
Each dollar owed costs more in local currency
Imports and energy cost more
Oil and many goods are priced in USD
Borrowing gets more expensive
Bond yields and default-risk premiums rise
Local central banks hike too
To defend the currency, slowing the economy
Research question
The Fed raises interest rates. Is that bad news for emerging markets?
1.3% → 2.9%
The 2-year U.S. Treasury yield, Sep 2017 – Nov 2018 (approx.), as the Fed kept hiking
≈10%
Average fall of emerging-market currencies against the dollar: a fairly mild reaction
So what decides whether a hike hurts? Why it happens.
Three reasons the Fed raises rates
01
The Fed turns hawkish
A shift in its reaction function: tighter policy for the same economy
02
Inflation rises
Prices are rising too fast, the Fed raises rates to cool demand
03
U.S. growth is stronger
A booming economy pushes rates up
Monetary shock
Tighter money worldwide and weaker U.S. demand: bad for emerging markets
Growth shock
Stronger U.S. demand offsets higher rates: mild
Interactive web embed: not captured for export
Example
Your Luckin coffee gets more expensive
¥9.9
¥12.9
Luckin just charges more
The U.S. just charges more
You just pay more
Emerging markets just pay more
= Monetary shock
Luckin is booming
The U.S. is booming
You pay more, but get more shifts
Emerging markets pay more, but get more exports
= Growth shock

Critique
Question everything, even the Fed
Not peer-reviewed
A 2020 working paper, revised and published in 2022.
The rule is too simple
Mood swings can be mislabeled as growth news.
Other shocks left out
Turkey’s and Argentina’s currency crises, and the U.S.–China trade war.
Still
The core result holds across four assets and both kinds of news.
Takeaways
Ask why the Fed is tightening, not just whether
1
Monetary news (a hawkish Fed, inflation fears) hits emerging markets hard. Growth news barely does.
2
Stronger economies are hurt less by monetary shocks, and can even benefit from U.S. growth.
3
Inflation-driven tightening cycles are the dangerous ones for emerging markets.
